2. Platform Engineering

The Push for Playwright Tests

We're investing in end-to-end test coverage with Playwright. We've tried this before but it never took root. Now, more than ever, it is important to have thorough, high-quality tests. When the agent can generate & run tests as part of its workflow, automated E2E coverage becomes both more achievable and more valuable. It's a key piece of making the agent self-verifying, and it's what will eventually let us replace full-app manual regression testing on every release.

We're early here. But it's a priority, not a nice-to-have. E2E tests accelerates unlocks codebase-wide architectural refactors - without the automated tests, we'd have to manual test everything to a level of specificity we just won't be able to guarantee in a reasonable amount of time.

Codebase Architecture: Making Code Agent-Navigable

Context engineering isn't just documentation - the code itself is context. If the codebase has three different ways of doing the same thing, the agent will pick whichever pattern it encounters first, and you'll spend your review time catching inconsistencies instead of evaluating business logic. This is why we're treating architectural consolidation as a harness engineering investment, not a cleanup project.

Backend: Clean Layered Architecture. We're consolidating three divergent patterns into a single, consistent layered architecture: Database → Model → Repository → Service → Controller → Router. Each layer has a clear responsibility and a clear contract with the layers adjacent to it. The repository layer abstracts data access. The service layer contains business logic. The controller layer handles request/response orchestration. The router layer defines endpoints and groups them.

Permissions follow a defense-in-depth pattern across three levels: at the router level (authorizing access to a group of endpoints), at the controller level (authorizing a specific endpoint), and at the service level (authorizing a specific action & scoping all actions to a particular tenant based on the user generating the request). This layered authorization means the agent can't accidentally create an unprotected endpoint - the pattern enforces security at every boundary.

If this architecture sounds familiar, it should. It maps remarkably closely to the layered architecture OpenAI enforced in their harness engineering experiment (Types → Config → Repo → Service → Runtime → UI). That's not a coincidence - it turns out the same architectural patterns that make code navigable for new Engineers make it navigable for agents. Strict layer boundaries, predictable file organization, and consistent contracts between layers give the agent a reliable "mental"S model of the system. When every feature follows the same path through the same layers, the agent can reason about where to put new code without guessing & code review becomes simpler, too.

Frontend: From Batch-Load to Performant Data Fetching. On the frontend, we're migrating away from a legacy pattern that loaded the full application state upfront and then applied smaller incremental updates - a pattern that made sense when the application was smaller but now creates sluggish initial loads & complex state management. We're moving toward a more performant approach: fetching data when it's needed, where it's needed, with proper loading states and caching.

This isn't just a performance play. The legacy pattern was difficult for humans to reason about - and it's the same for agents. When state management requires understanding a global loading sequence and a web of incremental update paths, the agent has to hold an enormous amount of implicit context to make safe changes. The new pattern is modular & local: each component is more self-contained, data dependencies are explicit, and the blast radius of any individual change is smaller. That makes it dramatically easier for the agent to work in one area of the frontend without inadvertently breaking another.

Both of these refactors serve dual goals: a more responsive application for our users, and a codebase that gives Claude Code a solid, consistent foundation to build on. The first goal would justify the work on its own. The second makes it urgent.

Environment Strategy

We're investing in two related problems: making it trivially easy for non-engineers to set up local dev environments, and standing up ephemeral environments for every PR.

On the local dev side, a significant blocker to Designers and PMs vibe coding is the friction of environment setup. If it takes half a day and three Teams (yeah - MS Teams...) threads to get a local environment running, the "just prototype it" promise falls apart. We're streamlining this so that anyone with access to the repo can be running the app locally in minutes.

On the infrastructure side, we're moving toward ephemeral environments - one per PR is the goal. This removes a major coordination cost. Today, PRs contend for a limited set of shared test servers. With ephemeral environments, every PR can be reviewed, tested, and demo'd independently. This is especially important as PR volume increases - and it's a prerequisite for getting meaningful feedback from PMs, Designers, and customers before code hits the release branch.

3. Harness Engineering

If the process changes create the conditions, harness engineering is the actual multiplier. This is where platform & infrastructure work produces leverage for every Engineer on the team - because you're not just improving human workflows, you're improving what the agent can do.

Context Engineering: CLAUDE.md & Persistent Indexed Learning Repositories (PILRs)

CLAUDE.md: Every RIVET repository is getting a CLAUDE.md file - a structured project-level context document that gives Claude Code reliable direction on tech stack, an index to other files containing in-depth architecture literature, naming conventions, and some lite do's & don'ts. These are team artifacts - reviewed in PRs, evolved alongside the codebase, treated as seriously as any other infrastructure configuration.

Persistent Indexed Learning Repositories (PILRs): Following the OpenAI team's finding that a large instruction file actively degrades agent performance, we're treating CLAUDE.md as a map - not an encyclopedia. The real depth lives in knowledge bases and knowledge indices: structured documentation that agents can reference when working in the disparate domains of our system. The goal is to move Claude from "generic coding assistant" to "specialist who knows how RIVET's platform is built," without bloating the context window with information irrelevant to the current task.

We've setup a couple of Claude Skills to help us build out these "Learning Repositories." The idea is that we have an index file (read "json file") that categorizes types of knowledge & systems in a central location. This index file then references additional material (markdown files) in "Learning Repositories" (directories full of information on a specific system). This allows the Engineer to guide the agent to the right information for working with a specific sub-system. During the course of the work, the agent will learn more about the system - or even change the system. This results in an update to documentation.

Rules and Hooks

Rules, and eventually hooks, are how you move from "the agent sometimes does what I want" to "the agent consistently follows our process." They're the mechanical enforcement layer of the harness.

Rules are constraints and conventions that the agent follows automatically - coding standards, naming patterns, file organization, things the agent should always or never do. These live alongside the CLAUDE.md and evolve with the codebase. Note: these are loaded into context by the agent at session start. Rules are a "human-level" abstraction. The agent reads all of the rules & mashes the stuff together into a big context window. Frontmatter can help negate this, but PILRs are the real way to get the information to the agent without bloating its context window.

This is where the OpenAI harness engineering findings hit closest to home. Their key insight: if an architectural constraint matters enough to document, it matters enough to enforce mechanically. Documentation that isn't enforced will drift - especially when agents are generating code at high volume. We're moving in this direction, encoding our conventions as rules rather than relying on engineers to remember and the agent to infer. The aspiration is what OpenAI demonstrated: linter error messages that double as remediation instructions, so every violation guides the agent towards a solution.

Hooks trigger automated actions based on agent behavior - for example, running linters after code generation, or auto-formatting files. We haven't fully leveraged hooks yet, but they're on the roadmap as the next layer of automation. Combined with rules, hooks are how you build the kind of continuous mechanical enforcement that the OpenAI team credits as a key multiplier - constraints that apply everywhere at once, without human attention.

Caveat: The agent follows the examples it sees in your codebase. If you have a Rule that instructs the agent to use a specific pattern but your code base compliance to that pattern is sparse, the agent won't use the pattern consistently. You must refactor your existing code to be the example of what your future code should be.

Skills

Skills are reusable capabilities you give the agent - packaged workflows that can turn complex, multi-step workflows into a single command. At RIVET we are prolific skill builders. We have skills for reviewing code, building PILRs, fixing specific types of bugs, implementing fullstack features, rewriting the commit history on a branch for human-readability, and many more usecases. One of my favorites is the /implement skill, which builds a small feature using a Spec-Driven Development workflow, saves information about the specific implementation plan in an ephemeral (gitignored) directory, creates a test plan, writes the code for the feature & then runs automated & manual tests. It sometimes also successfully takes screenshots of the UI during testing & references those screenshots in the PR. Here's how it works:

We already have PRDs (written by PMs) and Tech Specs (written by Engineers) for any non-trivial feature work. The /implement skill utilizes these & creates a Project Plan - a breakdown of the work to be done based on the current codebase and the desired outcome laid out in the PRD & Tech Spec. Engineers review the project plan before moving on. The project plan includes a step-by-step breakdown that maps directly to the commits for the PR.

Engineers are expected to break work down to PR-sized chunks. Giving the agent work that's too complex results in poor outcomes and slows everything down. The /implement skill is not a silver bullet for one-shotting entire system re-writes. That said, I frequently start with a feature that is too large for the /implement skill, hit a wall & then break the work down into smaller chunks for the agent to work on.

A Test Plan augments the project plan. Also written by the agent, it details both the new automated tests to be written and the manual testing steps. After the agent writes the code, it leverages the test plan to perform manual testing - using cURL for endpoints & the Claude Chrome Extension for UI testing. The agent takes screenshots and adds them to a gitignored folder to help build the PR. This is our version of what the OpenAI team calls agent observability - giving the agent the ability to see and interact with the running application, not just the code. OpenAI wired Chrome DevTools Protocol into their agent runtime for the same reason: any validation that requires a human to inspect the running application is a bottleneck.

Finally, the /implement skill writes a pr.md, fills it out based on a template, and references the screenshots for the Engineer to use when opening the PR.

Claude Code's plan mode is built for this workflow. SDD dramatically improves output quality, but more importantly, it forces the hard thinking to happen before implementation rather than during it.

Note: I find myself updating the project plan, test plan & pr.md frequently while working on a specific PR. To help with this, we also have a /update-project-docs skill!

The Support Bot Agent

One of our most concrete wins so far is the support bot agent - a separate repo that we use across our repositories for solving support issues: customer-reported bugs, CS-escalated problems, and production issues that come in through our ticketing system.

The problem it solves is straightforward. Support tickets are a constant stream of small, context-heavy tasks. An Engineer picks up a ticket, spends twenty minutes understanding the bug report, another twenty finding the relevant code, and then some amount of time actually fixing it. The understanding & finding phases are where most of the time goes - and they're exactly the kind of work an agent with good context can compress dramatically.

The support bot agent has access to our codebase, our CLAUDE.md context, and the patterns we've documented for common issue categories. When a support ticket comes in, the agent can triage it - identify the likely affected area of the codebase, pull up relevant context, reproduce the issue where possible, and either propose a fix or surface the information an Engineer needs to fix it quickly.

The real unlock is a PILRs - we have a persistent directory in the support bot repo of previously solved problems with an index file that the agent can reference. This allows the agent to quickly identify patterns and solutions that have worked in the past, and apply them to new problems. It also allows us to build a knowledge base of common issues and solutions that can be used to train new agents.

The result: our support ticket throughput has measurably improved. We run two-week support shifts, and the backlog maintained per shift has dropped significantly. Engineers on support duty spend less time on the investigation phase and more time on the judgment calls that actually require a human - is this the right fix? Does this need a deeper architectural change? We've "re-purchased" half a developer because the Support Engineer gets half of their time back to work on feature development or lower priority bugs that wouldn't have been fixed until we did an "all hands on deck bug bash" (which happens about twice a year for 1 sprint).

This is also a good example of the "amplifier" dynamic in practice. The support bot works well because we invested in the context layer first. Without good CLAUDE.md files and documented patterns, the agent would just be guessing. With them, it's operating with genuine knowledge of our system.

Automated Code Review

Our review process has four layers:

Architectural review (human, before code is written). More complex systems go through a written tech spec process; less complex features get by with a lighter-weight conversation and bullet-point list of key architectural decisions.

Automated review (CI, during PR). /review-pr skill, SonarCloud analysis, GitHub Copilot code review, linting, and our test suite - all running through GitHub Actions. We get these checks to pass before asking a human for review.

Human code review & manual QA (during PR). Focused on the new feature, based on the test steps in the PR. One challenge: without ephemeral deploys, reviewers are contending for shared test servers. With AI, we can get through code and prototype features so quickly that we need an environment per PR. Sometimes you want feedback from people working in different functions (Product, CS, Marketing, Sales) - or from customers - before releasing.

Full application UAT/regression testing (on the release branch). At the end of every sprint, all Engineers, Designers & PMs run through a half-day UAT marathon on the release branch. We log bugs, prioritize them & fix them in the first week of the next sprint. The quantity of bugs we're finding during this process is reducing every sprint - a testament to the effectiveness of the first three layers of review. We're working toward replacing this with automated Playwright tests.

What's Not Working… Yet

The context debt problem

Writing good CLAUDE.md files and knowledge bases takes real time. There's a bootstrapping cost - you have to document things that lived only in Engineers' heads, in a format useful to an agent, while also shipping product. We underestimated this significantly.

Our emerging solution: Persistent Indexed Learning Repos (PILRs). These are files that the agent updates as it develops a deeper understanding of the system - indexed via something like an index.json that maps topics to specific documentation files. The idea is to balance context window efficiency (the agent doesn't need to load everything) with maximum access to the most relevant information when it's needed most. Instead of requiring Engineers to write all the context documentation upfront, PILRs let the context accumulate organically as the agent works in the codebase.

This is the same architecture OpenAI converged on independently. They found that a single large instruction file actively degrades agent performance - it crowds out the task-relevant context. Their solution was a short AGENTS.md (~100 lines) that points to deeper sources of truth in a structured directory, with background agents scanning for stale documentation and opening cleanup PRs. PILRs are our version of this pattern, with the added benefit that the agent itself builds the knowledge base over time rather than requiring Engineers to write it all upfront. It's still early, but it's the most promising approach we've found to the cold-start problem.

The review bottleneck is stickier than expected

The Faros data predicted this. We still underestimated the cultural friction around smaller PRs.

Part of the issue is that agentic development makes it much easier - and more emotionally rewarding - to create large PRs. You feel like you're getting a lot done. The agent just built an entire feature end-to-end. The overhead of breaking up the PRs feels like it's not worth it.

But there's also a deeper cultural issue: Engineers who are used to shipping large, self-contained chunks of work often don't yet see the value of single-unit work streams. The argument is straightforward once you've experienced it - decreased friction means greater unit velocity, easier-to-review and easier-to-test PRs mean better quality, and smaller blast radius means fewer side effects - but it's a habits change, not a tooling change. It takes longer than updating the Claude CLI when a new model drops.

We don't have clean attribution data yet

We're tracking PRs per week, projects per quarter, points per sprint, and support ticket throughput... but not all in perfect ways. We're working on getting better at this & seeing a lot of improvement, but it's not there yet. We're planning to move toward proper DORA metrics to get a clearer picture of what's working and what's not.

Multi-agent Parallelization

We have some of this going on using GitHub Copilot, the Support Bot Agent and running 1-3 tasks locally at any given time. I’ve read some pretty sensational claims from companies like Ramp & Stripe. We don’t have things tuned to the level that these companies purport & I haven’t figured out how to multiplex my brain, yet. We’re not operating in the “multi-agent nirvana” future.

What You Can Do This Week

If you're reading this and wondering where to start, here's a practical first week:

Read the docs. Start with the Claude Code documentation. Understand what's possible before you start building on top of it.

Write a CLAUDE.md for one of your repositories. Start with your tech stack, your architecture in two paragraphs, and three things you wish every new Engineer knew before touching the codebase. It will force you to articulate things that have never been written down. That discipline pays off whether or not the AI ever reads it - and it's the first step from individual AI productivity to team AI productivity.

Start experimenting with rules and skills. Once the CLAUDE.md is in place, try adding a rule or two - coding conventions, file organization patterns, things the agent should always or never do. Then try writing a simple skill for a workflow you repeat regularly.

Download and use the Claude Chrome Extension. Use the agent to see & interact with your running application. It's a meaningful step up from terminal-only interaction. It's what makes the self-testing workflow in our /implement skill possible.

Try the Superpowers plugin. This Claude Code plugin gives the agent the ability to read and interact with web pages, take screenshots, and validate its own work in the browser. I used it to build detroitdevelopers.com - the site hosting this very post - largely in a single session. It's a force multiplier for anything with a visual component.

None of this requires a BHAG or an executive mandate. It requires a week of focused experimentation - and the willingness to be bad at something new before you get good at it.

Phil works at RIVET, building software to ensure the right people are on the right job at the right time. This post reflects lessons from an experiment still in progress.

entry.title: Getting Started with AI Agents in Production
entry.content:
AI agents are transforming how we build software. In this post, we'll explore the fundamentals of deploying AI agents in production environments.

What Are AI Agents?

AI agents are autonomous systems that can perceive their environment, make decisions, and take actions to achieve specific goals. Unlike traditional chatbots, agents can use tools, maintain state across interactions, and handle multi-step workflows.

Key Considerations

When deploying AI agents in production, there are several important factors to keep in mind:

  • Reliability - Agents need fallback strategies when tool calls fail
  • Observability - You need to see what decisions the agent is making and why
  • Cost management - Token usage can scale quickly with complex agent workflows
  • Safety - Guardrails and human-in-the-loop patterns are essential

Getting Started

The simplest way to start is with a single-purpose agent that handles one well-defined task. From there, you can expand to multi-agent architectures as your confidence grows.

Stay tuned for our upcoming panel discussion on Agentic Software Development on March 23rd!

entry.title: Project Management for Software Development: How to deliver more value, more faster
entry.content:
Note: this is an old post, ported from my old blog. I originally wrote it for a talk I gave at the Detroit Software Developers meetup on September 10, 2025. The process described here is how RIVET worked at that moment; it has kept evolving since.

Introduction

Who is Phil?

Engineering Manager @ RIVET Work; previously @ early-stage startups, mid-stage scaleups & late-stage large orgs.

Why is project management important for software startups?

VC-backed startups are unique. If they don't grow at exponential rates, they go out of business. The intensity of "the game" is very high - big risk & bigger rewards.

Well managed projects deliver value & everyone wins. Poorly managed projects result in missed goals & everyone loses (culminating in lack of growth, down-sizing & eventually shutdowns).

Thinking about exponential growth - a game: You have a pond in your backyard. This pond has lots of beautiful & interesting flora & fauna in it. One day you notice a Lily Pad growing. The next you notice two Lily Pads. You know you can't let the Lily Pads take over the entire pond because they'll consume too many resources & decimate the other life in the pond. But you're busy & the Lily Pads are pleasant to look at, so you don't do anything about them at first. On the third day there are four Lily Pads in the pond. Every day after, the rate of growth remains constant. On the 20th day, half of the pond is covered with Lily Pads. How many days do you have to take care of the Lily Pads before they cover the entire pond?

(One. That's the thing about exponential growth.)

What is RIVET Work?

RIVET is an early-stage B2B SaaS startup HQ'd in downtown Detroit. At RIVET, we're building a construction labor operating system for specialty contractors (e.g., Electricians). Construction labor management is a highly technical discipline. Making high-quality, intuitive software to help professionals manage this process is difficult.

The purpose of this post

I'll walk you through how RIVET manages projects, organizes our product team & delivers software that our customers love. I'll also sprinkle in improvements to RIVET's process that I'm experimenting with. My goal is to share practical takeaways you can apply in your own teams.

How to ship more, faster - a philosophy

💡 Insight: Focus on shipping value

I see companies fail to deliver enough value to customers quickly enough due to 3 root causes:

  • Failure to ship the Right Things™️
  • Shipping the Wrong Things™️
  • Not shipping (often enough)

Shipping quickly doesn't matter if you're shipping the wrong things. Prioritize addressing these problems in this order:

  1. Maximize shipping the Right Things
  2. Minimize shipping the Wrong Things
  3. Ship (often)

How to ship the Right Things

You don't know what the Right Things are

Plan in iterations of increasing refinement:

  • Business-level Goal: Start with a business outcome you'd like to achieve (this is often handled at the executive level).

    • Example: "Increase revenue by $x before y date through increasing unit price by $x via adoption by markets/user personas a & b"

  • Product Initiative: Define product direction based on business goals (often handled by Product Management).

    • Example: "To increase adoption of the a market, we will build features x, y & z"

  • Project Goal: Projects should deliver a slice of the Product Initiative (the sum of many projects is a product initiative).

    Example project goal

  • Milestones: Projects will have many milestones. Milestones are project-specific & should be logical slices of project delivery.

    • Example: "Feature X clickable prototype" or "Feature X in alpha for internal user acceptance testing"

  • Sprint Plans: A sprint plan can be as simple as a list of experiences you plan to demo (and release) at the end of the sprint.

    The whole project's sprint plan gets re-cut every week or two

    Example sprint plans

  • Story Tickets: Story tickets should be written by the Product Manager/Owner & detail the needs of the end user that are being met by this feature. They are usually feature-sized & consist of multiple PRs to finish. Don't size story tickets, or size them loosely (e.g., T-shirt sizes).

  • Task Tickets: Task tickets should be written by the role doing the work (e.g., the Engineers on the team) & should culminate in completion of a Story Ticket. You may have a DB task, a backend task, an infra task & several FE tasks that together complete a Story Ticket. Size task tickets with more granularity than Story Tickets (e.g., Fibonacci points).

You know what the Right Things are, but you aren't shipping them

Embrace change by making scope changes "free". When a change is requested, prioritize it for a future project or reduce scope from the current focus.

  • You can only do this if work is visible
  • You can only make work visible if work is at least roughly planned. Maintain a product backlog with a 🔭 zoomed-out view (quarters) & a 🔬 zoomed-in view (tickets)
  • Do not change focus mid-sprint (unless absolutely necessary). This one trips up non-engineers: context shifting kills the productivity of deep work (like design & coding).

How to avoid shipping the Wrong Things

What are the Wrong Things?

  • Things no one actually needs (a failure in discovery & convergence)
  • Things that are bad (bugs, tech debt that slows you down too much later, a feature that is good but has bad UX)

How to avoid shipping the Wrong Things?

  • 🎯 Figure out what the Right Things are & do those things instead
  • 🏎️ Quality built-in
    • DORA metrics
      • Deployment Frequency
      • Lead Time for Changes (merge to deploy)
      • ⭐ Change Failure Rate (rate of bugs) ⭐
      • Mean Time to Recover (MTTR)
    • Build trust with non-technical stakeholders by delivering results (ship the right things, often). Your non-technical stakeholders don't understand "Tech Debt", but they will understand that it's important if they trust you & you think it's important

How to ship quickly

Levers: thinking in iterations

  • Concurrency: Run iterations concurrently (stand up more teams & run more projects simultaneously)
  • Iteration Performance: Shorten iteration time by using small batches (1-4 weeks is ideal)
  • System Performance: Accomplish more value per iteration, requiring fewer iterations total to reach the end goal (ship only the next most valuable things)

Iteration performance maxing: small batch size

  • 1-4 weeks is good; 2 weeks seems to be a "sweet spot" for most teams I've worked on
  • Ship what you planned to ship at the end of the cycle
  • Don't change course mid-cycle (unless you're going to crash)

⭐ System performance maxing: aggressively obliterate scope creep ⭐

The biggest issue I see pop up time & time again is what I call "Kitchen Sink Scope Creep".

Kitchen Sink Scope Creep: When you're working on a system/feature that is adjacent to another system/feature that could also use some attention, so you are now working on two things simply because they are adjacent. This process compounds over time so that soon you are working on four things, then eight, sixteen, etc.

Analogy: You're repainting a kitchen & The Boss walks in and says "while you're in here, the sink needs to be replaced, too!"

This is great because you've discovered a new need. However, if you try to replace the sink while painting you will end up with bad outcomes. And it could be that the sink doesn't need to be replaced at all (maybe it's a nice-to-have that is now being prioritized over everything else, like fixing the toilet & repairing the lock on the front door). The Boss feels that you should deliver both the paint & the sink together now because they've been staring at the sink every time they come in to check on the painting progress.

Solution: Finish painting. While you do that, plan the new sink installation with The Boss (what kind of sink do they want? what did they not like about the old sink?) by creating a story ticket in the backlog of the project (or even a new project). This way the sink replacement is documented & there is work being done on it (discovery & convergence), but the painting project is not immediately at risk because your team is trying to demo the old sink (dust) & test piping (water) while painting (bad outcomes when interacting with dust or water). Just as important, the kitchen sink can now be prioritized in line with other priorities instead of jumping the line ahead of much more important features (e.g., the front door lock).

💡 Insight: Anytime scope is added mid-sprint or mid-project, said scope is implicitly prioritized above everything else that comes after this sprint & after this project.

Hard Truth: Prioritization & scope creep reduction is really difficult because it is a multiplayer, zero-sum game. Scope that is removed can be personally offensive to people (e.g., a design experience, a specific user request, an executive pet project/feature). The only way through it is by building trust with stakeholders & bringing them to your side. Many tough conversations are ahead. Enlist the help of your PM.

How can I ensure I ship every cycle when feature delivery can take longer than 1 sprint? Release ≠ Launch

  • Release: Code is released to Production (feature flags, experience toggles, new features that don't disrupt existing experiences, feature skeletons, component libraries, prototypes)
  • Launch: Feature is turned on in GA (feature flag removed, new experience enabled, users trained)

🧠 Takeaway: Focus on shipping value

  1. Ship the Right Things
    • 🤑 Make changes "free" by trading scope instead of adding hours or extending the deadline
    • 🔄 Iterative planning process
  2. Don't ship the Wrong Things
    • 🎯 Ship the Right Things instead
    • 🏎️ Quality built-in (sell it as a way to prevent future disruptions)
  3. Ship quickly
    • 🥃 Small batch size
    • 🚱 Efficient cycles (only prioritize the next most important things for delivery)
    • 🚀 Frequent releases; purposeful launches

How RIVET builds product (with some seasoning) 🌶️

💡 Insight: Software development is a process of iterative refinement

The Pipeline: Discover → Converge → Deliver

Our product development pipeline runs on three verbs:

  1. Discover (What & Why)
    • Tools: ProductBoard + Notion
    • Inputs: Customer feedback, sales insights, market research, analytics, business goals
    • Owners: Product Managers
    • Output: Clear priorities that are valuable to customers
    • Checkpoint: 🏔 Product Steering Committee (every 12–18 weeks) for big-picture alignment. We use this to set quarterly goals.
  2. Converge (How)
    • Tools: Figma + discovery interviews (2–3 per week)
    • Owners: Product Designers, with engineering + product input
    • Output: Tested prototypes, "Figma-as-spec," validated solutions
    • Checkpoint: ♠️ Betting Table (every 2 sprints) where we decide what's ready to move into delivery. We use this to set sprint goals for the length of a project.
  3. Deliver (Who & When)
    • Tools: Notion + GitHub
    • Owners: Engineering Manager + Engineers, with continuous input from design & product via demos (WIP/pre-recorded demos, sprint demos)
    • Output: Working software, released
    • Checkpoints: 💈 Backlog Grooming (weekly) + 🧭 Sprint Planning (bi-weekly). We use these to ratify near-term sprint goals.

The Battle Rhythm

  • Steering Committee (quarterly)
  • Quarterly Goal Setting & Product Initiatives (quarterly)
  • Project Launch (monthly)
  • Product & Application Metrics Review (monthly)
  • Customer Empathy Indoctrination (monthly)
    • Types: PM-led (UX), SME-led (market), "Game Film" (customer calls)
  • Sprint Planning (bi-weekly)
    • PMs should bring groomed Story Tickets to Tech Leads ahead of Sprint Planning
    • Tech Leads bring Task Tickets & (updated) Sprint Plans to Sprint Planning
    • 💡 The entire project has its full sprint plan updated as an input for every Sprint Planning session
  • Internal Demos (bi-weekly)
    • Product Team demos: design progress, new devops features, API endpoints
    • Company-wide demos: features in varying grades of fidelity
  • Retros (bi-weekly)
  • Backlog Grooming - Story Tickets (weekly)
  • Standups (daily)

🧠 Takeaway: Software development is a process of iterative refinement

  1. Discover > Converge > Deliver: Start 🔭 zoomed-out & 🔬 zoom in each cycle
  2. Battle Rhythm: Follow the plan with discipline
  3. Adapt to your needs: This process works for RIVET at our current stage, but the process is far from what it was 6 months ago & will evolve over the next 6+ months

What can you do tomorrow to deliver more value, more faster?

Ship the Right Things & don't ship the Wrong Things

  1. Make work visible by building & maintaining a backlog
  2. Have a conversation with your stakeholders about Kitchen Sink Scope Creep. Find a way to gather & compile new needs without implicitly reprioritizing every time a "Kitchen Sink Replacement" opportunity arises (use the backlog you built in step 1)
  3. Embrace gradual refinement by employing Sprint Plans. Plan ahead more than your next sprint, even if the plan is low fidelity past a few weeks out. Update this plan every 1-2 weeks.

Ship often (every 1-4 weeks at a minimum)

  1. Release with rhythm: do whatever is necessary to release every x weeks. Shipping builds trust & you can't combat scope creep without trust.
  2. Utilize iterations when releasing: release things that help you learn & demo in production, even if they are behind a feature flag. Add more to your release in future iterations. Stop iterating & move on to the next most important thing once you've met your original goal.

🧠 Takeaway: Software development is a process of iterative refinement

entry.title: RosieBot: MCP in action at RIVET
entry.content:
Note: this is an old post, ported from my old blog. I originally wrote it for a talk I gave on July 16, 2025. MCP & the tooling around it have moved a long way since, so treat the specifics as a snapshot. It's the hands-on follow-up to A Framework for Building AI Features in SaaS Applications.

Thesis: AI fills product gaps & AI features are product-feedback mechanisms built into your product

SaaS companies (e.g., RIVET) will start to use AI (chatbot interfaces) to…

  1. Fill gaps with easy-to-implement (low-quality) product development experiences powered by a chatbot interface
  2. Plan high-quality product development experiences informed by customer usage of the chatbot interface
  3. Expose chatbot interfaces powered by data integrated from other products to provide customer value enabled by that data

Strengths:

  1. 💬 Flexible interface (NLP) - fills gaps
  2. 📊 Usage patterns - feedback over millions of possible product outcomes

Weaknesses:

  1. ❌ "Good enough" is often not enough:
    • Accuracy
    • Consistency
    • Convention vs Configuration
  2. ❌ Distribution (MCP is filling a gap, but there's a lack of easy setup for AI features)
  3. ❌ Advanced use cases need a sophisticated user (not everyone is a prompt engineer)

The chatbot has a place, but it is limited: Users want to achieve outcomes. They crave focused solutions to their problems - they don't want to ask the bot to design the dashboard every time, they just want the best dashboard for their problem. Once the AI novelty wears off (it already has for many), users will grow impatient with the "Chatbot UI for Everything" model.

Data Types: Peripheral vs Contextual

Peripheral Data

Peripheral: Generally available data (I can scrape this data off of a website without logging in)

  • public API docs
  • public marketing materials
  • product training resources
  • sales collateral

Contextual Data

Contextual: Data with context on the specific user & use case (the user must be authenticated)

  • the user's own usage data (what did the user do right before querying the bot, which features does this user use most/least often, what is the user's persona)
  • the user's data in the app (e.g., the user's org's workers, jobs, assignments)

MCP: What is it & how does it work?

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a pre-agreed upon standard for structuring communications between models (LLMs) and tools (operations over datasets). MCP can be used to help AI devs create Agents.

💡 MCP unlocks contextual data 💡

Think "REST for AI"

Data access for AI apps

An AI app like Claude can't see your customers' data in your product. An MCP server gives it a set of tools it can call to go get that data on the user's behalf. Here's Claude calling a RIVET get_all_job_reports tool to answer a question about my jobs (and the tool failing, which will be a theme):

Client-server design

User → MCP Client → LLM
                  → MCP Server → Tools (e.g., external APIs)

The MCP client sits in the middle. It tells the LLM which tools exist, the LLM decides which tool (if any) would help answer the query, & the client asks the MCP server to actually run it.

Ecosystem alternatives

  • Function Calling
  • Vectorized DB access
  • A2A

How to get started?

  • Assuming you have public APIs
  • Set up an MCP client & server
  • Implement inter-service auth
  • Tune your settings
  • Figure out that your public APIs are not suited for this type of data access
  • Create purpose-built APIs for MCP
  • End up using vectorized data pipelines instead (haha jk)

RosieBot: MCP Deep Dive

RosieBot is a chatbot I built into RIVET (a labor planning & scheduling platform for construction contractors) as a prototype. You ask it questions about your jobs & workers; it uses MCP tools backed by RIVET's public API to answer.

Example usage

When it works, it's great. Against seeded data:

Seeded data - success case (tool arguments redacted). Look closely & you'll see the dates don't agree between the first half of the answer & the second.

When it doesn't, it politely tells you to go use the product:

Failure case

System architecture

There are four moving parts:

  • RIVET Web Application (RWA): the UI the user types into
  • RIVET Web Service (RWS): RIVET's API, which also hosts the public API
  • RIVET MCP Client (MCP-client): talks to the LLM & the MCP server
  • RIVET MCP Server (MCP-server): exposes tools that call RIVET's public API

Request cycle

  1. The user enters a query into the RIVET Web Application UI (RWA)
  2. RWA sends the query to the RIVET Web Service (RWS)
  3. RWS authenticates the request, checks permissions & scopes the request to the current user's org
  4. RWS sends the query to the RIVET MCP Client (MCP-client)
  5. MCP-client adds some "magic sauce" (prompt context & the tools list) to the query & sends it to the LLM to see if the LLM thinks any of the tools will help it process the request
    • MCP-client gets the tools list from a prior registration handshake with the MCP-server
  6. The LLM uses NLP to understand the query & selects a tool to help it answer the query. It then responds to the MCP-client with a tool use request
  7. The MCP-client authenticates the tool use request (in this case, with the requesting user's token) & forwards the tool use request to the RIVET MCP Server (MCP-server)
  8. The MCP-server processes the request by calling on external data sources (in this case, the RIVET public API hosted on RWS) & returns data back to the MCP-client
  9. The MCP-client sends this data to the LLM
  10. The LLM determines if it has sufficient context to answer the question
    • If no, the LLM makes an additional tool use request to the MCP-client (this ends up being several responses)
    • If yes, the LLM processes the query & returns a response to the MCP-client
  11. The MCP-client stitches the responses together from the LLM & returns them to RWS
  12. RWS returns the response to RWA
  13. RWA formats the response & displays it to the user

Lessons Learned

Good surprises

  1. Setup was not very difficult - if you already have APIs to get started with
  2. I spent <$5 on credits testing this over a week, & the API key comes with $5 of free credits

Bad surprises

Getting a good (accurate & consistent) result was very difficult:

  1. Tool calls often exceeded the model's context window limit - I needed to make the data lean & specific
  2. I needed to create MCP-specific API endpoints to get data the LLM could use optimally
  3. Prompt engineering matters - a lot
  4. Fixing issues with maths or other specific domains requires additional tool calls (call the calculator tool instead of having the LLM guess the maths)

The Future - Where is this going?

RosieBot primary use cases

1. PM in my pocket

A request we've heard: "I want a PM in my pocket" via a phone app. One path there: AI apps like Claude let users plug in their own integrations, so RIVET's tools could show up in an app that's already on their phone:

2. Product-development feedback based on customer usage of the NLP input UX

Every question a customer asks the bot is a feature request in disguise. The log of what people ask for (& where the bot fails them) tells the product team where a focused, high-quality experience is worth building.

3. AI application integrations

Meet customers in the AI apps they already use by exposing RIVET's data to those apps through an MCP server.

Other use cases?

RIVET has job labor planning, worker scheduling & job performance data.

  • PM in a pocket
    • "Who has worked with JANE DOE over the last 30 days?"
    • "How can I get capacity for OPPORTUNITY X? Who could I move around to make them available for OPPORTUNITY X?"
    • "Who is scheduled to work on JOB Y at the end of this week?"

entry.title: How to get your team to prioritize tech debt
entry.content:
Note: this is an old post, ported from my old blog. I wrote it in April 2025 as the outline for a talk, memes & all.

1. Why is this a problem?

  • Trade-offs are hard.
  • Sprint points feel like a zero-sum game. Every point spent on tech debt is a point not spent on a feature someone is waiting for.
    • But it isn't actually zero-sum: less tech debt = greater efficiency in the future. The hard part is making that future efficiency visible to the people weighing it against a feature they can see today.

2. Understand your stakeholders' needs

Treat your PM, designer, EM & leadership the way you'd treat users: figure out what they need before you pitch them a solution. Start with a question: what does "tech debt" mean to the non-technical (or just other) stakeholders?

It's amorphous. It lacks a clear definition, or language to discuss trade-offs.

  • Solution: break tech debt down into "benefits" for an informed discussion of trade-offs. The conversation isn't "new feature or tech debt", it's "new feature or this specific performance improvement".

It has a reputation for being a black hole.

  • "It'll take 2 - 52 weeks to do this", or "it'll take 1 quarter" & then it takes 3 quarters.
  • It's typically worse before it's better, OR you have to overhaul a whole pattern across the entire codebase to get the benefit (a huge initial investment, or living with multiple patterns).
  • Solution: break down the problem (planning!) so you can give a realistic estimate & options (people love options).

3. Choose your path

1. 🌉 A culture that supports tech debt

  • The PM & EM trust engineering ICs to do the right thing. They don't need to know the ins & outs of the specific work & focus; they just trust you'll do the right thing.
  • This is really hard to achieve because you have to build up this trust by consistently doing the right thing in their eyes & for the business.
  • Popular for eng-run companies & small orgs that are extremely profitable / successful. It's easy to ask for budget when the money is flowing.

2. (Collaborative) non-compliance

  • It's not endorsed, but you can either just prioritize it & tell others to kick rocks, or
  • you can prioritize it without making it clear that you're working on it.
  • Popular for all orgs.

3. 🪣 Tech debt budgets

  • 20% of everyone's points per sprint, or
  • 1 sprint per quarter, or
  • 1 in 5 people focused 100% on tech debt
  • Popular for big orgs.

4. 💡 Redefine "tech debt" in a language the team can collaborate on

Ad hoc tech debt projects.

  • Tech debt is a huge category. Be very specific with your ask. Make each piece of tech debt its own project.
  • There's friction per instance, but you can now have an informed discussion of trade-offs.

5. ⭐ Break the false dichotomy of choice & mix 'n' match 1-4

You don't have to pick one. A budget gives you room to plan; specific, well-defined projects make the trade-offs discussable; delivering on both builds the trust that gets you closer to path 1.

4. Conclusion

  1. Empathize with your collaborators (PMs, Designers, other engineers).
  2. Build trust to help the cultural focus on tech debt & trade-offs improve.
    • DO NOT act in bad faith (non-compliance).
    • DO budget for tech debt. Start by using this time to define tech debt & plan how to solve it.
    • DO redefine tech debt: make trade-offs obvious.
      • Fair warning: this may result in not prioritizing some tech debt.
    • DO plan your tech debt removal so you can give accurate estimates.

entry.title: A Framework for Building AI Features in SaaS Applications
entry.content:
Note: this is an old post, ported from my old blog. I originally wrote it for a talk I gave on April 10, 2025. AI moves fast, so read it as a snapshot of how I was thinking about AI features at the time. A few months later I wrote about building one of these features for real in RosieBot: MCP in action at RIVET.

Introduction

Who is Phil & why does he care about AI?

  1. I'm an Engineering Manager at RIVET. Previously I held titles such as "Software Engineer", "Lead Engineer" & "Founding Engineer" at Quicken Loans (pre-IPO), StockX (Seed & Series A), Procore (pre-IPO) & Portex (Pre-seed & Seed).
  2. I specialize in 0-to-1 & 1-to-n product development, with skills in Engineering, Product Management & team building.
  3. I've used a myriad of AI systems & built exactly 1 AI-enabled feature. I'm trying to learn more about this to build more AI features. I am an expert in product development, but by no means an expert in AI.
  4. My interest in AI is centered around:
    • Me: How can I use this to make my life/job easier? (vibe coding, copilots, image generation, trip itinerary planning)
    • Users: How can I use this to build useful features into my products?

What is AI?

  • A computer program that uses an LLM to reason (make decisions)
  • Some of these programs are advanced enough to act out a subset of the decisions that they make ("agentic")
  • The LLM is the result of an ML process

What is the scale of AI?

  1. There are 2 phases: the short tail (now - ? months) & the long tail (? months - years in the future)
  2. AI is a revolution (think agricultural, trades, industrial, computer, internet, smart phone, etc). It is impressive. The short tail is firming up (chat interfaces as a big player). The long tail will blow our minds.
  3. In this post, I'm going to focus on the short tail & what we can build now as application developers, especially as SaaS app developers.

Why do we need an "AI Features Framework"?

  1. There are a finite number of AI feature categories that are being built in SaaS apps today. This will change some time in the future (maybe tomorrow, maybe in 5 years).
  2. Cataloging the finite quantity of features available today helps product teams focus on what they can build to benefit customers & where they can explore (push the boundary).

Thesis: SaaS companies (e.g., RIVET) will start to use AI (chatbot interfaces) to…

  1. Fill gaps with easy-to-implement (low-quality) product development experiences powered by a chatbot interface
  2. Plan high-quality product development experiences informed by customer usage of the chatbot interface
  3. Expose chatbot interfaces powered by data integrated from other products to provide customer value enabled by that data

The Framework

The framework has two parts:

  1. "Rails": Environmental Constraints
  2. "Building Blocks": Feature Categories by Ability
    • Example Use Cases
    • Environmental Form ("Rail")
    • Data Sources

"Rails": Environmental Constraints

How tightly does the environment constrain what the AI actor can do? I think of it as states of matter:

  1. Gas: Environments where the AI actor can operate with limited constraints. Any constraints are usually offered in the prompt/instructions to the AI or at the model-level, and therefore not changeable without switching models. No ML expertise required.
    • Example: basic image generation based on a user-provided prompt
  2. Liquid: Environments where the AI actor can operate with moderately firm constraints. These constraints are often inexpensive to change but require some engineering effort. Very little ML expertise required.
    • Examples: modifying data in an application in a pre-defined way via an API; retrieving data from a pre-defined data source such as a database or website homepage
  3. Solid: Environments where the AI actor can operate with severely strict constraints. These constraints are often expensive to set up & change. Changes to the functionality of the feature cannot be achieved without physical "rails" changes and/or advanced ML expertise.
    • Examples: self-driving car lanes, automated factory production lines, fine-tuning models using self-learning feedback loops

"Building Blocks": Feature Categories

These are the "Lego blocks" of AI products today. Each has an ability, example use cases, the rails it needs & the data it runs on.

1. (Unpredictable / Dangerous) Data Mutation, aka Generative AI

  • Example use cases: Prototyping, asset creation, document drafting
  • Environmental constraints: Gas Rails. Requires very little in the application environment on top of the base model to get started, but can expand greatly depending on how the application's users expect generation to work (e.g., generate a song vs generate a specific type of image vs generate a fullstack application)
  • Data sources: Static - e.g., an uploaded image, a chat prompt, a document with great detail on a plot for a book to be generated

2. Query (relatively) static data

  • Example use cases: Query static documents such as API documentation
  • Environmental constraints: Gas Rails. Requires static data to be fed into the application environment on top of the base model - e.g., via web scraping based on a URL or OCR of a document
  • Data sources: Static - e.g., product documentation, API documentation, customer help articles or a website's home page

3. Query dynamic data

  • Example use cases: Query an application for answers to questions involving my company's proprietary data in the SaaS application
  • Environmental constraints: Liquid Rails. Requires an interface (today, these are APIs for real-time & data streams for close-to-real-time) with usage instructions to perform approved queries
  • Data sources: Malleable - e.g., a transactional database that is hosting individual end user data (today these are queried via API for certainty)

4. Self-improving system (model fine-tuning)

  • Example use cases: Netflix's movie recommendation engine, an ever-improving project schedule builder, a personalized tutor that "learns" the best way to help me learn
  • Environmental constraints: Solid Rails. Requires a continuous feedback loop such as an ML engine fed by end user feedback - implicit (did the user pick this option or keep searching?) or explicit (thumbs up & down)
    • Note: requires model fine-tuning, which is an advanced ML practice & compute-intensive
  • Data sources: Malleable - feedback from the system's key metrics

5. (Safe) Data Mutation: agentic workflows to perform specific actions based on reasoning informed by input data

  • Example use cases:
    • "Show me options for flights from A to B on date X. Book flight Y using my credit card."
    • "Why can't I schedule more field labor? Oh, I don't have enough seats in my subscription. Increase my subscription amount using my saved billing info."
    • Self-driving cars in specific self-driving car lanes, or in specific cities that have municipal codes & streets mapped out in a way that an algorithm can take advantage of
    • "Dark Factories" where AI-enabled manufacturing machines perform actions based on very strict physical constraints
  • Environmental constraints: Solid Rails. Requires an interface (e.g., an API) with usage instructions to perform approved actions. These systems aren't AGI; they are an algorithm-behind-a-curtain that appears to be very smart.
  • Data sources: Malleable - e.g., sensor inputs, APIs returning data from a database, documents representing streets or a schematic for a widget to be built

These categories become more valuable for end user experiences when combined.

Two kinds of data: peripheral & contextual

The data fetch blocks above split along one more line that matters a lot for effort:

  • Peripheral data: public or pseudo-public data about an application & its service offerings (marketing materials, sales materials, public API documentation, user training materials). Chatbot providers like Chatbase, Ada & Intercom can ingest this out of the box via PDF upload, copy/paste, wiki integrations & website crawlers. Little to no engineering effort.
  • Contextual (in-app) data: the customer's own data in the application. This needs an API or database integration, which means real engineering effort to build & maintain.

Applying it: what could a SaaS app like RIVET build?

RIVET helps construction contractors plan & schedule their field labor. Here's how the building blocks map onto features for a product like ours.

1. Sales/Marketing chatbot (data fetch - peripheral)

  • Benefit: lets prospects learn about the product & service offerings on demand, & surfaces learning materials such as podcast bites, webinar clips & e-book excerpts
  • Effort: can be set up out of the box with existing chatbot providers. Very little to no engineering effort required.
  • User: customer prospect

2. Support chatbot

  • v1: data fetch - peripheral
    • Benefit: customers get on-demand answers to simple questions about use cases, training & documentation without waiting on a human. Should allow seamless escalation to human support.
    • Effort: out of the box with existing providers
    • User: active customer
  • Later: (safe) data mutation
    • Benefit: "Why is there a banner on my account? Oh, I haven't paid? How can I pay? Approve a transaction on my card on file."
    • Effort: significant, because it needs purpose-built APIs & integration, & the self-serve features underneath it have to exist first

3. In-app product chatbot

  • v1: data fetch - in-app
    • Benefit: customers get information about their specific data (e.g., "There is a severe weather warning for Southeast Michigan this Friday. Who is working on jobs in Southeast Michigan this Friday & Saturday?")
      • fills gaps in the current product experience with a low-quality interface
      • informs the product team of areas to focus on for high-quality interfaces to replace the chatbot
    • Effort: moderate, due to the need for API or database integration
    • User: active customer
  • v2: (safe) data mutation - in-app
    • Benefit: customers take specific actions on their data, such as "message everyone scheduled on jobs in Southeast Michigan this Friday with this content & show it to me before sending so I can approve it"
    • Effort: significant, due to the purpose-built APIs required

Example Product Roadmap

Putting it in order of delivery:

  1. AI data fetch with access to peripheral data (product help articles, podcasts, marketing material, API documentation)
    • Service customer questions about the product in sales, training & support contexts
  2. AI data fetch with access to contextual data (specific customer data in the database)
    • Unlock many new customer-driven query features
    • Use the queries customers generate in this feature to inform future product development experiences
    • Expose query features against imported partner & competitor datasets that help capture market share
  3. AI (safe) data mutation
    • Unlock many new customer-driven mutation features
    • Use the mutation queries customers generate in this feature to inform future product development experiences
    • Expose more features against imported partner & competitor datasets that help capture market share

Within step 2, the freshness of the data is its own ladder, & each rung costs more engineering than the last:

  1. Manual exports of customer data fed to the chatbot. Limited data, not real-time, no engineering effort.
  2. "Slow" in-app data: automated, batch-processed document-style exports. Still limited data, close to but not real-time. Significant engineering investment to implement & maintain.
  3. "Quick" in-app data: automated, batch-processed exports to a vector data source. Data size is no longer the chief constraint. Massive engineering investment.
  4. "Real-time" in-app data: change data capture streaming into a vector data source. 🙂 Massive engineering investment, & then some.

Technical challenges

While there are many products that offer chatbot interfaces informed by specific APIs (e.g., Chatbase) or document uploads (e.g., Pinecone Assistant), there are no systems with plug-and-play database integrations. The systems that exist today provide RAG services. Plug-and-play database services would require extremely massive & complicated document RAG implementations OR a data pipeline system that moves data into a vector database that the agent has access to.

entry.title: Evolution of Data Pipeline Software Architecture at RIVET (2020 - 2025)
entry.content:
Note: this is an old post, ported from my old blog. I originally wrote it for a talk I gave at the Detroit Software Developers meetup on February 27, 2025. The company numbers, team sizes & "future" plans are all a snapshot of that moment.

Intent: A software architecture journey via a real-world case study on how a software startup grew & how the software architecture evolved to support the business' growth.

Method:

  1. What a data pipeline is & how it works at a high level
  2. What RIVET is & how a data pipeline helps solve problems at RIVET
  3. Evolutionary history of software architecture at RIVET
  4. A vision of what the future holds for RIVET's business & how the software architecture will evolve to meet the business' needs

Introduction

What is a data pipeline?

According to AI: A "data pipeline" is a series of automated processes that move data from its source to a destination, often involving transformation and cleaning steps along the way, to prepare it for analysis and further use, essentially acting like a conveyor belt for data within a system; it allows organizations to collect, process, and deliver data from various sources in a structured manner for insights and decision-making.

According to Phil: A "data pipeline" is a tool used to move data from one place to another place.

For a good visual overview of both the low-res (ETL) & high-res versions of a data pipeline, watch ByteByteGo's What is a Data Pipeline? | Why is it so popular? (there's also a 60-second version).

Why should I care?

Data pipelines allow you to achieve:

  1. Business-scale, high-speed decision making across multiple datasets.
  2. Functionality you just can't do without the data from multiple datasets.
    • Venmo can't work without data from the sender & receiver's banks.
    • RIVET can't work without data from your bidding system, project management system, employee system, employee certification system & accounting system.

If you have several systems that your business relies on (e.g., HubSpot, Salesforce, Jira, Notion, GitHub, QuickBooks, etc) & want to take action informed by data in more than one of these systems at a time, then you will probably benefit from a data pipeline.

This isn't just about having data on a screen that helps the [human | AI] operator make a choice somewhere else. The best case is the data is in the system where the decisions are being made.

RIVET's business model & why data pipelines are important

What is RIVET?

RIVET is a seed-stage, B2B SaaS startup in the construction tech industry, HQ'd in Detroit. Started in 2020. At the time of this talk we were at 42 employees with 15 in Product & Engineering:

  • Engineers: 8
  • Engineering Managers: 2
  • CTO: 1
  • PMs: 1
  • Director of Product: 1
  • Product Designers: 2

Our stack: TypeScript, Node, React, Azure, K8s, Docker, Terraform, BullMQ, Redis & Postgres.

Customer: Construction subcontractors involved in skilled trades (e.g., Electrical, Plumbing, Mechanical, etc). Specifically the "Labor Coordinator" & "Project Manager".

Customer problems

  1. Labor Coordinator: As a Labor Coordinator at a skilled-trade Subcontractor, you have to manage the daily-shifting schedules of 100s-1000s of workers across 100s of job sites. If (when) you make mistakes, the wrong people show up to the wrong job sites. This hurts the company's profitability (because the people are still paid) & turns the job site managers (Foremen) into your enemies. You currently use Excel, a whiteboard & your phone to do this job.
  2. Project Manager: As a Project Manager at a skilled-trade Subcontractor, you are responsible for the profitability of the jobs under your management. You ensure your jobs are profitable by planning how the job is executed & then reviewing performance against your plan (usually by looking at % complete vs total cost to date). You must review & revise your plan every week for every job (someone shows up to the wrong job site, someone is sick, someone quits or is fired, someone takes time off, the entire job schedule is pushed because of a delay with another subcontractor, etc). You use Excel, an ERP/Accounting report & some project management software to do this job.

Solution: A software tool that allows you to match the optimal worker to the job & communicate this match across your company.

Why does RIVET need a data pipeline?

Why use a data pipeline for anything?

  1. You need to get data from multiple systems into 1 system to help you make decisions
  2. You own the 1 system where decisions are made & you need to get your customers' data from multiple systems into your 1 system

RIVET is the platform where construction Labor Coordinators & PMs are making people & project scheduling decisions. In order to make these decisions, they need data on people & projects. This data usually lives in 3-5 separate places, half of which they may not have access to without RIVET.

In order to help our customers achieve the solution above, RIVET needs to provide information about the:

  1. Jobs: address, customer, financials, type of project
  2. Workers: address, emergency contact info, pay rate / cost to company (~2x pay rate), experience, trade, classification
  3. Worker Certifications: title, date attained, experience date, description, image/artifact
  4. Job Schedules: start & end dates, what type of work is needed on the job & when
  5. Worker Schedules: specifically who joins the job to fulfill the required work & when

🤯 Each type of data lives in a separate system:

Source Systems
Jobs ERP, Accounting, Bidding Software
Workers HRIS
Worker Certifications Excel, Google Drive
Job Schedules Excel, P6
Worker Schedules RIVET

Because all of the data that RIVET needs to work is maintained in other systems, RIVET needs a way to ingest this data. Options:

  1. Manual data entry: Some customers will do this; most won't
  2. One-time import (& then manual data entry to maintain): Some customers will do this; most won't
  3. Automatic data updates: 💰💰💰

Past: Prologue

1. The Prototype: SFTP

Snapshot: Q2 2022

Company: Pre-seed · ~$2.6m raised · ~6 employees
Data: 100s of records going through the data pipeline · 1 integration
Data team: CTO: 1

Andy Lawrence, Co-founder & CTO, created the original data pipeline for our first "big" customer. We call this the "ETL Service" because it:

  1. Extracts files from our (or their) SFTP site
  2. Transforms the data based on customer business logic per customer
  3. Loads the data into our public API

System topology

Coded transformation configs

Example coded ETL config

How do RIVET transformation configs work? TS configuration files control how a series of functions processes data.

  • Fetch Logic: How to get the data (SFTP server info, API endpoint auth info, fetch/poll frequency)
  • Skip Logic: Callback with rules run for each record in the incoming data set. If the return value is true, that record will be skipped from further processing
  • Field Ignore: Source of truth / create vs update
  • Key Mapping: hireDate, re_hire_date → hiredate
  • Formatters: Callback transforms the given field

2. The First Iteration: ODBC

Snapshot: Q4 2022

Company: Pre-seed · ~$2.6m raised · ~10 employees
Data: 1,000s of records going through the data pipeline · <5 integrations
Data team: CTO: 1

Another customer needs ODBC extraction, so Andy extends the SFTP prototype with three more components: the "Data Agent Client", "Data Agent Service" & "Data Agent Admin".

The Data Agent Client is a .NET application that can be installed on customer servers (for security or cost-saving purposes) or RIVET-hosted (for ease of use & lower customer maintenance burden) that runs SQL queries against customer databases on a configurable frequency.

The Data Agent Service is a Node application for managing Data Agent Clients installed on RIVET VMs & customer servers. The data available to be managed includes: SQL queries to be run, the SQL query frequency, the source database connection credentials, the destination URL & API token, and various other options relevant to the system.

The Data Agent Admin is an internal React application used to manage Data Agent Clients via the Data Agent Service.

System topology

ODBC connector: Data Agent Admin UI

Data Agent Admin UI

3. The Data Pipeline Team begins to form & tooling gets an upgrade

Snapshot: Q1 2023

Company: Pre-seed · ~$2.6m raised · ~12 employees
Data: 1,000s of records going through the data pipeline per day · ~10 integrations
Data team: CTO: 1 · Engineers: 1

I'm hired & promptly put in charge of onboarding new customers' data into RIVET as well as extending the data pipeline's capabilities. Over the next 24 months, a team of several engineers, a designer & a PM is built to help support this function (and other responsibilities).

  • Creating & maintaining customer integrations mostly happens via SQL queries in the Data Agent Service & coded configs in the ETL Service
  • We deploy a Data Agent Client on a RIVET VM so we can connect to customer cloud-based databases without installing the Data Agent Client on their machines (which was often a time suck)
  • We start to invest in internal tooling to help us better monitor & manage customer integrations & our data pipeline
    • RIVET CLI for ergonomic access to relevant data about a single "transaction" through the data pipeline
    • Metabase for dashboards & metric aggregation

System topology

Internal tooling

We found that building new integrations was simple, but debugging running integrations was difficult. We tried many approaches to this, such as making it easier to deploy them in a sandbox environment where customers could review them before promoting to production, & making local development easier. One solution we landed on was creating an internal CLI tool for viewing the data flow between the different system components (Data Agent Service → ETL → Public API), which helped us debug issues (see where data fell off / had an issue). In order to do this, we used a tracerId (uuid) that tied all of the data around the end-to-end transaction together.

Here's roughly what a trace looks like (anonymized & trimmed):

% rivet trace -u <tracerId>

---
Found: <tracerId>
[
  {
    "name": "rivet-hosted-agent",
    "hasRequest": true,
    "hasResponse": true,

    "status": 17
  }
]

---
Found: <tracerId>

  {
    "name": "agent_customerName_StateCode",
    "transactionStatus": 7,
    "streamStatus": 5,

    "recordsSucceeded": 250
  }
]

  {
    "name": "Customer Name [PRODUCTION]",
    "endpoint": "/v1/jobs",
    "resStatusCode": 200,

  }
]

We also built dashboards to help us visualize the health of the entire system & get more visibility into specific issues.

Metabase (customer config names redacted)

4. The Second Iteration: HTTP

Snapshot: Q3 2023

Company: Pre-seed · ~$2.6m raised · ~12 employees
Data: 10s of thousands of records going through the data pipeline per day · ~100 integrations
Data team: CTO: 1 · Engineers: 1 · PM / Engineer: 1

Louis Gelinas, Co-founder, First Developer & Director of Product @ RIVET, builds the first HTTP extraction using the "Not HTTP Service", aka the "HTTP Connector".

The HTTP Connector periodically polls external APIs to extract JSON data using a customer-provided API key. The first one was a coded, per-integration fetcher: authenticate with the 3rd party API, page through the results, transform them & hand them to the ETL Service.

System topology

5. GUI Tooling: CSSI

Snapshot: many iterations throughout 2024

Company: Seed · ~$9m raised · ~30 employees
Data: 100-300k records going through the data pipeline per day · 100 integrations at the start, 427 as of this talk
Data team: Engineering Manager: 1 · Engineers: 1 - 3 · PM: 1 · Designer: 1

We started to build a GUI tool for configuring integrations in Q1 2024. This tool is called "Customer Success Configured Integrations" (CSSI).

  • DB-based integration configurations: CSSI moves the transformation logic from code to the database, which unlocks a UI to customize transforms per customer.
  • Manual file upload: CSSI also supports manual file upload, which allows for easier testing of data payloads & replaces our "bulk uploader" functionality.
    • We start to use manual file uploads for integrations that were SFTP, but were not automated exports & uploads to our SFTP server (so a customer had to upload using an SFTP client like FileZilla).
  • Dry Runs: The data pipeline now supports "dry runs", which allow testing an integration in production & getting a snapshot of changes without committing the changes.

CSSI UI

List of integrations in the CSSI UI

Configuring an integration in the CSSI UI

System topology

Present: Where we are today

6. RIVET Data Services

Snapshot: Q1 2025

Company: Seed + Bridge (mini A) · ~$15m raised · 42 employees
Data: 100s of thousands of records going through the data pipeline per day · 427 integrations
Data team: Engineering Manager: 1 · Engineers: 3 · PM: 1 · Designer: 1 · Director of Data Services: 1 · Integration Developers: 1

Data Services Team: CSSI enables integration specialization apart from engineering. Data technicians can now create & maintain integrations without needing to write & deploy code.

RIVET context

System topology

The topology is the same as the Q1 2024 diagram in the CSSI section above.

Infra hosting & setup

  • Azure VMs, Application Gateway
  • PM2
  • Nginx
  • Async jobs for messaging (SMS, email, in-app notifications) via BullMQ (Redis + TS)

Future: The RIVET data pipeline of the future™️

Problems: Reliability, Performance & Operations

  1. Acute Problem - Throughput (a performance issue leading to a reliability issue): The data pipeline would not process jobs (batches of data) as quickly as it was receiving jobs. This led to a theoretical processing time of infinity. Most customers had 1-hour SLAs, some had 5-minute SLAs. The data pipeline was slow, but for our customers it appeared down.
  2. Operations: As we migrate from "Engineers write integrations" to "Data Services Integration Developers write integrations", we need more robust tooling for debugging issues with integrations. Put another way: Engineers can dive into our prod SQL databases & ssh into VMs to discover issues; Integration Developers must use the tools provided by our Data Pipeline Engineering team.
  3. Long-tail Performance: With new customers & new data types, we plan to increase load on our data pipeline infra by 50-100x (quantity of records, not quantity of data) over the next 36 months.
  4. Tenant Isolation: Noisy tenants shouldn't affect their neighbors by clogging up the queue for everyone.
  5. etc, etc, etc - the list goes on

Solutions: Strategy Documents, BullMQ & Record-level Metrics - Oh My!

  • ✅ Better Visibility: More clarity on service health & bottlenecks
  • ✅ Horizontal Scaling: More workers to process data
  • ✅ Strategy Docs: We wrote a Data Pipeline Technical Strategy for Q1 2025.
    • Benefits: Helps us know what to do & in what order, builds trust with other teams & parts of the business, and gives us a framework for adjusting our plans over time.
    • Pillars: Definition · KPIs · High-level Plan · Immediate Next Steps
  • 🏗️ BullMQ: Queues help with reliability
  • 🌄 Record-level Metrics: Metrics per record instead of per batch of 100s of records

Metabase

Closing
